PINS AdvantageDeep endorsement wording checks inside ProcoreYes, wording levelYes, from contractsYour teamYesYes
TrustLayerA large vendor network and broker partnersYesYesAI, confirmed by a personYesFree tier only

How we compared them

We looked at the same six things for every tool, in this order of weight:

  1. Endorsement review. Does it read the additional insured, waiver of subrogation and primary and noncontributory endorsements against your requirements, or only the certificate?
  2. Requirements by project. Can each project carry its own limits, endorsements and exceptions?
  3. Broker in the fix. When a subcontractor COI falls short, how does the contractor's broker learn what's missing, and where do they send the fix?
  4. Monitoring after approval. Renewal requests, expirations and changes to coverage mid-project.
  5. Who makes the final call. AI on its own, your team, or a managed service. AI COI tracking varies most here.
  6. Construction fit and pricing. Procore and construction accounting integrations, and whether you can see COI tracking software pricing before a sales call.

The best COI tracking software for construction, tool by tool

1. Forsured: best for checking every COI against the project it's for

Forsured is construction insurance compliance software for general contractors, trade contractors and the brokers who insure them. You set your insurance standards once, then apply project-level requirements and exceptions where a job needs them. Forsured reads each certificate and endorsement against that project's requirements and flags each gap with the reason, such as a missing ongoing operations additional insured endorsement (CG 20 10) or an umbrella below the required aggregate. The broker gets the gap in a shared workspace where they see the requirement, the document and the project, instead of another email chain. After approval, Forsured keeps tracking renewals and coverage changes across active projects. AI finds and explains each issue, and a person on your team approves or waives it.

Good fit if your projects carry different owner, lender or contract requirements, you want the broker working from the same requirement you are, and you want a person on every approval.

Watch for: onboarding is by waitlist, the Procore integration is for early access customers and isn't on the Procore Marketplace yet, and there's no managed review service.

Pricing: not published. Forsured offers a free COI risk check: send one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two, and they'll show you every gap.

2. bcs: best for published per-vendor pricing and a free tier

bcs have tracked insurance certificates since 2008, for property managers, general contractors, risk managers and procurement teams. Requirement templates can be set by vendor type, project or property. Their AI reads each certificate twice, with a long-running extractor and a separate vision model, and sends any disagreement to a person. AI endorsement review identifies the endorsement type and walks you through it with an endorsement matrix. On the full-service plan, US-based analysts handle outreach and call the vendor and, when needed, the vendor's insurance agent, with no cap on attempts.

Good fit if you want to start free, see rates up front, and keep the option of handing outreach to a service.

Watch for: bcs isn't built only for construction, and full policy and description of operations review comes with full service, which carries a $10,000 annual minimum.

Pricing: free up to 25 vendors with every software feature. Self-service is $11.40 per vendor per year. Full service starts at $17.80 per vendor per year with a $10,000 annual minimum.

3. Billy: best for COIs, lien waivers and payroll in one construction tool

Billy are COI tracking software for construction only: general contractors, developers, owners and homebuilders. Beyond COIs, they track prequalification, certified payroll, lien waivers and warranties through closeout. Each requirement is set per project, and their AI checks each COI for missing endorsements like CG 20 10, CG 20 37 and waiver of subrogation. Renewal requests go out three months before a policy expires, one month before, and on the day. Compliance status can sync to your accounting system to hold a payment before the check run. You can run it yourself, or use their managed plan, where CRIS-certified reviewers check every certificate and endorsement.

Good fit if you run Procore with a construction ERP such as Sage, Viewpoint Vista, CMiC or JD Edwards, and want payment holds tied to compliance.

Watch for: brokers fix gaps from a deficiency list and an upload link rather than a shared workspace, and there's no full price list.

Pricing: plans start as low as $500 a year and scale with the number of vendors and the plan. A free trial is available.

4. Certificial: best for live policy data from the agent of record

Certificial work differently from the rest of this list. Certificates come only from the vendor's agent of record, through a network of more than 25,000 agencies, and the agency's system keeps each certificate current. That lets Certificial flag mid-term cancellations and limit changes as they happen rather than at the next renewal. Their EndorsementIQ pulls the carrier, form number, policy number and exclusions from each endorsement so you can accept or reject it against your criteria, and a project layer handles more than one set of requirements. Agents and brokers use it free.

Good fit if you run a large vendor program and want to hear about a cancellation the day it happens.

Watch for: there's no Procore integration on their site or the Procore Marketplace, the product is aimed at enterprise and procurement teams rather than construction, and live data depends on the vendor's agency being on the network.

Pricing: free for up to 5 suppliers. Professional starts at $99 a month. Enterprise is quoted.

5. illumend (formerly myCOI): best for letting AI make the call on high volume

illumend is the AI platform from myCOI, who've worked in third-party insurance compliance since 2009 from Indianapolis. The old mycoitracking.com address now redirects to illumend, and myCOI customers are being moved over. Their AI, Lumie, reads every line of each COI and endorsement, from additional insureds and waivers of subrogation to primary and noncontributory wording and per project aggregates (see what per project aggregate means on a COI), and decides whether the language meets your contract. It raises a hand only on items it can't resolve, and follows up with vendors and their brokers until gaps close. In Procore, illumend builds the agreement from a commitment and rechecks the certificate at renewal.

Good fit if you track a high volume of vendors across more than one industry and you're comfortable with AI COI tracking that decides on its own.

Watch for: requirements follow the contract rather than separate project-level requirement sets, the Procore Marketplace listing still carries the myCOI name, and more human oversight is an add-on.

Pricing: not published.

6. Jones: best for GCs that also own or manage real estate

Jones serve commercial real estate owners and property managers as well as construction general contractors, from New York. AI and Jones's insurance specialists review COIs and endorsements, and the Policy Review add-on reads full policies for exclusions a certificate won't show. Requirements can be set by record, project or property, and in Procore you can track insurance at the project or company level. The Operator tier adds a concierge team that handles the back-and-forth with brokers, agents and third parties.

Good fit if your company builds and also owns or manages property, and you want exclusions in the full policy reviewed.

Watch for: most broker follow-up sits in the Operator tier, Policy Review is charged per policy, and rates aren't published.

Pricing: per tenant or vendor record per property, billed annually, with unlimited COI reviews for each record. Quotes come from sales. Jones never charges your vendors or subcontractors.

7. PINS Advantage: best for deep endorsement wording checks inside Procore

PINS Advantage started with a California insurance agent supporting commercial contractors. PINS reads every certificate and endorsement against requirements built from your contracts, shows its reasoning and the page it came from, and goes into the wording: whether a CG D3 81 meets a CG 20 10 and CG 20 37 requirement, for example, or whether privity of contract language limits who's covered. Your team approves, rejects or waives every result. In Procore, PINS reviews each COI against the requirements tied to the commitment and writes Approved or Not Approved back to the project directory and the commitment's compliance tab, which Procore Pay uses.

Good fit if Procore is the center of your workflow and you want Procore COI tracking with endorsement wording checked and a person on every decision.

Watch for: brokers respond through an upload link and revised endorsement requests rather than a shared workspace, and monitoring is renewal and expiration notices rather than live policy data.

Pricing: plans start around $300 a month with unlimited users and onboarding, and most annual contracts come in at $7,500 or less. There are no feature tiers, and the Procore integration is included.

8. TrustLayer: best for a large vendor network and broker partners

TrustLayer serve construction, real estate, retail, finance and other industries. Their Enhanced Endorsements feature checks for the language you require, including additional insured and common equivalents, primary and noncontributory, waiver of subrogation, and blanket versus scheduled endorsements, then shows the page that proves it, with a person confirming the result. Insurance can be tracked per project. Brokers get their own access, and some brokers resell TrustLayer and offer review services. Pulse verifies a policy at the source, and TrustLayer+ is their full-service option with licensed insurance professionals.

Good fit if your subs' brokers already use TrustLayer, or you want policy verification at the source.

Watch for: the Procore, CMiC and Vista integrations start at the paid Pro tier, and paid prices are by quote.

Pricing: free up to 50 vendors. Paid tiers are quoted.

COI tracking software pricing, side by side

COI tracking software pricing is usually set by how many vendors or certificates you track, and only some vendors publish it. Here's what each one shows before you talk to sales:

ToolFree optionPublished priceHow it's priced
ForsuredFree COI risk checkNoneBy quote, early access
bcsUp to 25 vendors$11.40 per vendor per year; full service from $17.80 with a $10,000 minimumPer vendor
BillyFree trialFrom $500 a yearBy vendors tracked and plan
CertificialUp to 5 suppliersProfessional from $99 a monthBy plan
illumendNone listedNoneBy quote
JonesNone listedNonePer record per property, annual
PINS AdvantageNone listedFrom about $300 a month; most contracts $7,500 a year or lessBy certificates tracked
TrustLayerUp to 50 vendorsNone for paid tiersBy quote

When you compare quotes, ask whether the price covers endorsement review or only the certificate, whether integrations cost extra, and whether your subs ever pay to upload. Low COI tracking software pricing that leaves endorsements to your team can cost more in staff hours than it saves, so the best COI tracking software for you isn't always the cheapest.

Procore COI tracking: who connects and how

Six of the eight tools are listed on the Procore Marketplace, and they do different things with the connection. For Procore COI tracking, ask where the status lands and whether it can hold a payment:

  • PINS Advantage reviews each COI against the commitment's requirements and writes Approved or Not Approved to the project directory and the commitment's compliance tab used by Procore Pay. The integration is included in every plan.
  • Billy syncs to Procore and a long list of construction accounting systems, and can hold payment before the check run.
  • Jones tracks insurance at the project or company level in Procore.
  • illumend creates the agreement from a Procore commitment, shows status on its insurance tab, and rechecks at renewal. Their Marketplace listing is still under myCOI.
  • TrustLayer tracks insurance per project in Procore, from the Pro tier up.
  • bcs connects to Procore alongside Yardi and MRI.
  • Forsured offers a Procore integration to early access customers, outside the Marketplace for now.
  • Certificial doesn't list a Procore integration.

Procore COI tracking only helps if the review behind it is right. A green status in Procore built on an unread endorsement is still a gap.

AI COI tracking: who makes the final call

Every tool here uses AI to read certificates. The real question with AI COI tracking is what happens after the AI reads it:

  • AI decides: illumend's Lumie makes each decision and only escalates items it can't resolve.
  • AI with a check: bcs reads each certificate twice and sends disagreements to a person. TrustLayer's endorsement review is confirmed by a person.
  • Your team decides: Forsured and PINS Advantage find and explain each issue, and your people approve, reject or waive it. Certificial extracts endorsement details for you to accept or reject.
  • Someone else's team decides: Billy's managed plan, bcs full service, Jones's specialists and TrustLayer+ put their reviewers on your certificates.

None of these is wrong. AI COI tracking that decides on its own moves fastest on volume. A person on every approval costs more time and leaves a clear record of who accepted a gap and why. Pick the model that matches who carries the risk at your company when a claim lands. For the endorsements that most often decide that claim, see whether additional insured status covers you after the job is done and what primary and noncontributory means on a COI.

Subcontractor COI tracking: how to choose

The best COI tracking software for one general contractor can be the wrong fit for the next. Before you book demos, answer these five questions about your own subcontractor COI tracking, and use the answers to narrow the list of COI tracking software for construction you'll see:

  1. Do your requirements change by project? If owners and lenders ask for different limits and endorsements, you need requirements set per project, with exceptions.
  2. Who reads the endorsements today? If nobody does, put endorsement review ahead of everything else on your list.
  3. How does a gap get fixed? Watch a demo of a deficient COI going to a broker and coming back corrected.
  4. Where do your teams work? If it's Procore, ask what Procore COI tracking status the tool writes back and whether it can hold payment.
  5. Software or service? Decide whether your team will review AI COI tracking results, or whether you'd rather pay someone to handle subcontractor COI tracking for you.

State rules matter too. Workers' comp thresholds and anti-indemnity statutes change what you can require, so check contractor insurance requirements by state before you build your templates.

About this ranking

This ranking was written by the Forsured team. Forsured makes one of the eight tools compared here and is listed first; the other seven follow in alphabetical order. No vendor paid to be included or saw this page before it was published. Every product, integration and pricing fact comes from the vendor's own public pages and the Procore Marketplace as of Nov 11, 2026. Prices and features change, so confirm them with each vendor. We didn't include review-site ratings.

item.title: Contractor backlog fell to 8.1 months. What it means for COIs
item.description: ABC's Construction Backlog Indicator dropped 0.6 months to 8.1 in October 2026. What the numbers say, and why thinner backlogs matter for contractor COIs.
item.content:encoded:
• ABC's Construction Backlog Indicator fell to 8.1 months in October 2026, down 0.6 months from September and 0.3 months from a year earlier.
  • The drop came from contractors without data center work. Their backlog fell from 8.3 to 7.6 months, while contractors with data center work rose from 11.3 to 11.5 months.
  • Infrastructure backlog fell to 8.7 months, its lowest since May 2025. Profit margin expectations improved, but sales and staffing expectations fell.
  • When backlog thins, more contractors bid on work outside their usual size or scope. Check that each contractor COI meets this project's requirements, not the contractor's last job's.

Contractor backlog fell sharply in October. Associated Builders and Contractors reported Nov. 10 that its Construction Backlog Indicator dropped to 8.1 months, down 0.6 months from September and 0.3 months from October 2025. For owners and GCs, a thinner pipeline means more contractors chasing each job, and that's worth a closer look at the COIs that come with the bids.

What ABC reported

"Backlog fell sharply in October, returning to levels not consistently observed since last winter," said ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu.

The split behind the number is stark:

GroupSeptemberOctober
All contractors8.7 months8.1 months
Contractors without data center work (88%)8.3 months7.6 months
Contractors with data center work11.3 months11.5 months

ABC notes that most contractors doing data center work have more than $100 million in annual revenue. By category, infrastructure backlog fell to 8.7 months, the lowest since May 2025, while heavy industrial backlog rose to a 15-month high.

The Construction Confidence Index was mixed. Profit margin expectations improved, while sales and staffing expectations fell. All three readings stayed above 50, the level ABC says signals expected growth over the next six months. Even so, Basu noted that "roughly 1 in 4 contractors still expect their margins to shrink over the next six months," citing recent increases in materials prices and borrowing costs.

Why it matters for contractor COIs

When backlog shrinks, contractors widen their search for work. That can mean bidding on projects larger than their usual jobs, in a new sector, or in a new state.

Their insurance was usually bought for the work they normally do. A program that fit a $10 million job can fall short on a $50 million one:

  • Limits. Umbrella and excess limits may sit below what a larger project requires.
  • Aggregates. A general aggregate shared across more jobs runs thinner. A per project aggregate keeps yours separate.
  • Endorsements. Additional insured, completed operations and waiver wording may not match the new project's contract.

None of that shows up in a backlog number. It shows up when you read each contractor COI against the project requirements for the job in front of you, not the contractor's last one.

Forsured checks every contractor COI against your project requirements and flags the gaps, so a competitive bid market doesn't bring a coverage gap with it.

item.title: What does per project aggregate mean on a COI?
item.description: A contractor's general aggregate is shared by every job it works. The per project aggregate endorsement, CG 25 03, gives your project its own. What to check.
item.content:encoded:
• Per project aggregate means the contractor's general aggregate limit applies separately to each designated construction project, instead of one limit shared by all of its work.
  • Without it, claims paid on the contractor's other jobs during the policy year reduce the same aggregate that's supposed to protect your project.
  • ISO's standard form is CG 25 03, Designated Construction Project(s) General Aggregate Limit. It covers ongoing operations and doesn't change the separate products-completed operations aggregate.
  • If your project requirements call for a per project aggregate, ask for the endorsement and confirm it designates your project, or all projects.

Per project aggregate means the contractor's general liability aggregate applies separately to your project. Without it, one aggregate limit covers every job the contractor works during the policy year, and claims on those other jobs use up the same limit your project is counting on.

What the general aggregate is

A general liability policy has two kinds of limits. The each occurrence limit caps what it pays for any one occurrence. The general aggregate caps the total.

IRMI defines the general aggregate as "the maximum limit of insurance payable during any given annual policy period" for covered losses other than specified exposures. Products-completed operations claims are "paid out of a separate aggregate." Once paid losses reach the general aggregate, "that limit is exhausted and no more losses in any of those categories will be paid."

That's the catch for an owner or GC. A certificate showing a $2 million general aggregate tells you what the contractor bought, not how much of it is left. A busy contractor with a bad year on two other jobs can show up to yours with far less.

What CG 25 03 changes

The ISO endorsement CG 25 03, Designated Construction Project(s) General Aggregate Limit, fixes that. IRMI says it makes "the general aggregate limit apply separately to each designated construction project," which "enables a contractor to comply with contractual requirements" for a specified amount of insurance on a specific project.

The form itself spells out how it works:

  • Each project gets its own limit. "A separate Designated Construction Project General Aggregate Limit applies to each designated construction project."
  • Claims stay in their lane. Payments for a claim tied to one project reduce that project's limit and "shall not reduce any other Designated Construction Project General Aggregate Limit."
  • Completed operations stay shared. Products-completed operations claims reduce only the products-completed operations aggregate. IRMI confirms the endorsement "does not affect the policy's other limits, including the products-completed operations aggregate limit."

A related form, CG 25 04, does the same for designated locations a contractor owns or rents, as Insureon explains.

What to check on a contractor COI

  1. Confirm your project requirements call for a per project aggregate, and at what amount.
  2. Look for it on the certificate, then ask for the CG 25 03 endorsement or the insurer's equivalent.
  3. Check the schedule. It should name your project, or say it applies to all construction projects.
  4. Remember completed operations. CG 25 03 doesn't separate that aggregate, so check its amount on its own.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against your project requirements, including the endorsements behind the limits shown, for the life of the job.

item.title: Insurance compliance is on the trades tech map. It's filed under getting paid.
item.description: Suffolk Technologies' new trades tech map puts insurance compliance under getting paid. Why it belongs at the start of the job, and why compliance isn't coverage.
item.content:encoded:
• Suffolk Technologies' November 2026 map groups emerging tools for trade contractors into five stages: win and staff work, run the business, plan and coordinate work, do the work, and get paid and manage cash.
  • Insurance compliance is on it, filed under payment compliance in the get paid stage, next to pay apps and lien waivers.
  • That placement matches how much of the industry runs it: as a gate on payment. By the time a payment is held, the crew has already been working with the gap.
  • Two shifts would make it a real operational gain: check coverage when a contractor is staffed onto the job and keep checking during the work, and test the coverage itself against the project requirements, not just the certificate's boxes.

Suffolk Technologies just published one of the more useful pieces of construction tech writing this year: A Better Tech Stack for the Trades. Its market map sorts the tools built for trade contractors into five stages of the job. Insurance compliance is on it, in the last column, under getting paid. We think that's an honest picture of how the industry runs compliance today, and a clear sign of where the next gain is.

What Suffolk Technologies mapped

The piece starts with the labor problem. Suffolk Technologies cites estimates of a skilled-labor gap of up to 600,000 U.S. workers, and notes that for every five people leaving the industry, only two enter it. Its answer is technology "designed around the way work actually happens" in the field.

The map, titled "Enabling the next phase of jobsite execution," follows a trade contractor through five stages:

StageWhat it covers
Win and staff workBidding and estimating, recruiting and training, safety and onboarding
Run the businessHR, payroll and crews, accounting, sales, financial intelligence
Plan and coordinate workProject intelligence, field collaboration, materials and procurement
Do the workField tools and diagnostics, automation and robotics
Get paid and manage cashPay apps and billing, payment compliance, working capital

Two arguments stand out. First, tech sprawl is real. The article says "the explosion of back-office tools is unmanageable in the long run." Second, the payoff is structural: modern tools let firms "move away from linear revenue to headcount growth." That's the right frame. The goal isn't more software. It's more work done per person, with less friction.

Where insurance compliance landed

On the map, tools for tracking certificates and prequalifying contractors sit in the payment compliance box, next to lien waivers and draw management. In other words, compliance is grouped with the paperwork that releases money.

That's accurate. On a lot of projects, the moment anyone looks hard at a contractor COI is when a payment is about to go out. If the certificate has lapsed or a requirement is missing, the payment waits until it's fixed.

The problem is timing. By the time a payment is held, the crew has already been on site, sometimes for weeks, working with the gap. If someone was hurt or something was damaged in that window, holding the check doesn't change who pays for the claim.

Move it to the start of the job

The map's first stage, win and staff work, already includes safety and onboarding. That's where insurance compliance belongs too. A contractor should prove its insurance meets the project requirements when it's staffed onto the job, before it mobilizes, the same way crews complete orientation before they start.

Then it should keep running in the do the work stage. Policies renew, change and cancel mid-project. A check that happens once at onboarding and again at each pay app misses everything in between.

Placed that way, payment becomes a confirmation, not a discovery. The pay app goes out on time because compliance was already clean.

From compliance to coverage

The second shift matters more. Most compliance work today confirms the paperwork matches a checklist: a certificate is on file, the additional insured box is checked, the limits are listed. As we've written before, compliance isn't coverage. A certificate can check every box and still leave the project exposed.

Coverage questions live in the policies and endorsements, not on the certificate:

  • Does the additional insured endorsement cover completed operations, or only ongoing work?
  • Is the coverage primary and noncontributory, as the project requirements say?
  • Is waiver of subrogation actually endorsed, or just typed on the form?
  • Do the umbrella limits sit over the right underlying policies?

Those answers decide who pays when something goes wrong. They're also the slowest part of the job to check by hand, which is exactly the kind of back-office work the article says the trades need to shed.

The bigger point

Suffolk Technologies is right that the trades deserve a better tech stack, built around the field. Its map already shows that insurance compliance is part of that stack. The next step is moving it from the end of the job to the start, and from checking paperwork to checking coverage.

That's the layer we're building at Forsured. If you want to see what it looks like on your own paperwork, send us one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two at hello@forsured.ai, and we'll run a free check.

item.title: Does additional insured status cover you after the job is done?
item.description: Since 1993, the standard ongoing operations endorsement stops covering you once the work is done. Why completed operations needs its own endorsement, and what to check.
item.content:encoded:
• Not with the standard ongoing operations form alone. Since ISO's October 1993 edition, CG 20 10 covers you only for liability arising out of the contractor's "ongoing operations."
  • Completed operations means work that's finished, or put to its intended use. Claims about finished work, such as a leak or a defect, need their own endorsement.
  • ISO's CG 20 37, first released in October 2001, adds the additional insured to the contractor's completed operations coverage. It doesn't cover ongoing work, so you usually need both.
  • On each contractor COI, ask for both endorsements, note the edition, and check how long your project requirements say completed operations coverage must last.

Not with the standard form alone. The ISO endorsement most contractors use to add you as an additional insured, CG 20 10, has covered only the contractor's ongoing operations since 1993. Once the work is finished, that endorsement stops responding. Coverage for finished work takes a second endorsement, CG 20 37.

Why the standard form stops at completion

The original 1985 edition, CG 20 10 11 85, covered liability arising out of the contractor's "your work," and that included both ongoing and completed operations. Construction Executive explains that ISO's October 1993 edition changed the wording to "liability arising out of your ongoing operations," which "effectively eliminated additional insured status for completed operations."

Insurance Journal put it plainly: "'Ongoing operations' does not include completed operations."

IRMI defines completed operations as work that "has been completed as called for in a contract," work finished at one jobsite of a multi-site contract, or work "that has been put to its intended use." In other words, a lot of the claims a GC or owner worries about. A roof leaks after turnover, or someone is hurt by a finished stair. Those arrive after the CG 20 10 stops covering you.

Where CG 20 37 comes in

ISO released CG 20 37 in October 2001. Construction Executive says the form's "sole purpose" was "to bring back the ability to add an additional insured to the completed operations coverage." Insurance Journal adds that it "does not provide coverage for ongoing operations."

So the two forms split the job in time:

EndorsementCovers you forDoesn't cover
CG 20 10 (since 1993)The contractor's ongoing operationsCompleted operations
CG 20 37 (since 2001)The contractor's completed operationsOngoing operations

The April 2013 editions of both forms added limits of their own. Coverage applies only "to the extent permitted by law," won't be "broader than that which you are required by the contract or agreement to provide," and is capped at the lesser of the contract's required amount or the policy limits.

What to check on a contractor COI

  1. Confirm your project requirements call for additional insured status for both ongoing and completed operations, and for how long after completion.
  2. Ask for both endorsements behind the checked AI box. Note each form number and edition.
  3. Check that the edition's limits fit your contract, especially the April 2013 language tying coverage to what the contract requires.
  4. Keep collecting certificates after turnover for as long as completed operations coverage must last.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against your project requirements, including the endorsement forms behind the AI box, for the life of the job.

item.title: Will a COI tell you if a contractor's policy is cancelled?
item.description: The standard ACORD 25 certificate doesn't promise to tell you about a cancellation. What the box says, what New York law adds, and how to get real notice.
item.content:encoded:
• Usually not. Since the 2009/09 edition, the ACORD 25 cancellation box says only that notice "will be delivered in accordance with the policy provisions."
  • Standard policy provisions send cancellation notice to the named insured, the contractor, not to the certificate holder.
  • New York's certificate law bars requiring certificate terms the policy doesn't contain, so adding notice wording to the certificate itself doesn't create it.
  • To get real notice, ask for an insurer endorsement that schedules you, and keep checking coverage for the life of the job.

Usually not. The cancellation box on the standard ACORD 25 certificate reads like a promise, but since the 2009/09 edition it only points back to the policy. And the policy usually sends cancellation notice to the contractor who bought it, not to you.

What the box actually says

Here is the current wording:

Should any of the above described policies be cancelled before the expiration date thereof, notice will be delivered in accordance with the policy provisions.

Older editions talked about mailing the certificate holder written notice within a stated number of days, though with a line saying that failing to do so imposed no obligation on the insurer or agent. The 2009/09 change dropped the days and handed the question to the policy.

So the real question is what the policy says. Standard cancellation conditions run between the insurer and its named insured. Unless an endorsement adds you, the owner or GC on the certificate isn't on that list.

Why the certificate can't fix it

It's tempting to ask the agent to type "30 days' notice to the certificate holder" into the description box. That doesn't create the right.

New York put this in statute. Insurance Law section 502 says a certificate "shall not amend, extend, or alter the coverage" of the policy it refers to, and "shall further not confer to any person any rights beyond those expressly provided by the policy." It also bars anyone from willfully requiring certificate language the policy "does not expressly include." New York's Department of Financial Services traces the rules to Article 5 of the Insurance Law, added in 2014 and 2015.

The certificate summarizes. The policy decides.

How to actually hear about a cancellation

  1. Ask for a notice endorsement. The fix is an insurer endorsement that schedules you to receive notice. BCS's example: "we agree to mail prior written notice of cancellation to the person(s) or organization(s) shown in the Schedule." BCS also warned these "are not generally available and are used sparingly by Insurers," so ask early.
  2. Track every policy period. Note each policy's expiration date from the COI and ask for a renewal certificate before that date, not after.
  3. Keep checking for the life of the job. A COI is a snapshot from the day it was issued. Put the check in your project requirements and repeat it, so a lapse shows up before a loss does.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against your project requirements and keeps checking for the life of the job, so a cancelled or expired policy doesn't hide in a file of old PDFs.

item.title: What does waiver of subrogation mean on a COI?
item.description: A waiver of subrogation stops a contractor's insurer from suing you to recover what it paid. What it means, where it comes from, and what to check on each COI.
item.content:encoded:
• A waiver of subrogation is the insurer's agreement not to recover what it paid on a loss from a third party, such as the owner or GC, after paying its own insured.
  • Insurers usually agree to it because their insured already gave up its own right to recover in a contract. The waiver shows that contract promise didn't void the coverage.
  • It comes from policy wording, usually an endorsement. The workers' comp form, NCCI's WC 00 03 13, applies only to parties named in its schedule and can be limited to work under a written contract.
  • On each contractor COI, match the waiver to the policies your project requirements list, and ask for the endorsement.

A waiver of subrogation is an insurer's agreement not to go after a third party to recover what it paid on a claim. On a construction project, that third party is usually you: the owner or GC. Without the waiver, a contractor's insurer that pays for a loss could turn around and sue you to get its money back.

What subrogation is

When an insurer pays a claim, it can step into its insured's shoes and pursue whoever caused the loss. In standard commercial policies, IRMI notes, that right sits in a condition called "Transfer of Rights of Recovery Against Others to Us."

A waiver gives that right up against named parties. IRMI explains that insurers usually agree to it because the insured has already waived its own right of recovery in a contract. Policies generally allow that waiver if it's made before a loss. Many exclude coverage if it's made after.

That's why construction contracts ask for it. The contract has the contractor waive its rights against the owner and GC. The insurer's waiver is the proof that promise didn't cost the contractor its coverage.

Where it comes from

Like additional insured status, the waiver comes from policy wording, not from the certificate. A checked waiver box on the certificate is only a summary.

On workers' compensation, the standard form is NCCI's WC 00 03 13, "Waiver of Our Right to Recover From Others Endorsement." Its key line: "We will not enforce our right against the person or organization named in the Schedule." Two details matter:

  • It's limited to the Schedule. The form says it "shall not operate directly or indirectly to benefit anyone not named in the Schedule."
  • It can be tied to a written contract. An optional sentence limits it to work done "under a written contract that requires you to obtain this agreement from us."

It can also cost extra. NCCI's instructions say a premium charge may apply. Tennessee's insurance department, for example, allows a carrier-set charge in the voluntary market and, for assigned risk policies, 5% of the related manual premium with a $250 minimum per waiver.

What to check on a contractor COI

  1. Confirm your project requirements call for the waiver, and on which policies: general liability, auto, workers' comp, umbrella.
  2. Ask for the endorsement behind each checked box. Note the form number and edition.
  3. Check that it names you, or applies to anyone a written contract requires, and that the contract is signed before work starts.
  4. Recheck at renewal, when endorsements can drop off.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against the coverage a project actually requires, including the endorsements behind the checkboxes, for the life of the job.

item.title: Is U.S. construction spending down? What the September 2026 numbers show
item.description: Census data released Nov 2 shows U.S. construction spending fell 1.9% in September 2026. Residential pulled it down while nonresidential grew.
item.content:encoded:
• Yes. U.S. construction spending ran at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $2,186.1 billion in September 2026, down 1.9% from August and 2.7% from a year earlier, the Census Bureau reported Nov 2.
  • Spending for the first nine months of 2026 was $1,649.6 billion, 2.9% below the same period in 2025.
  • Residential drove the drop: private residential spending fell 5.5% in the month.
  • Nonresidential kept growing. Private nonresidential rose 1.1% from August, and total nonresidential was 1.8% above September 2025.

Yes. U.S. construction spending fell 1.9% in September 2026, to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $2,186.1 billion, the Census Bureau reported Monday. That's 2.7% below September 2025. For the first nine months of the year, spending totaled $1,649.6 billion, down 2.9% from the same stretch of 2025.

The headline hides a split, though. Almost all of the decline is residential.

Where the drop came from

SegmentSeptember 2026 (annual rate)vs. Augustvs. Sept. 2025
Total$2,186.1B-1.9%-2.7%
Total residential$861.2B-5.4%-8.8%
Private nonresidential$790.6B+1.1%+2.3%
Total nonresidential$1,325.0B+0.6%+1.8%
Public$546.8B-0.1%+1.0%

Private residential alone fell 5.5% in the month, to $848.8 billion. Nonresidential, the work most commercial GCs and trade contractors depend on, is the part still growing.

On the public side, spending was essentially flat. Educational spending was $113.1 billion, virtually unchanged, and highway spending was $149.2 billion, down 0.3%.

These are preliminary numbers. Census revises each month, and August was revised in this release. The next update is due Dec 1.

What it means for project requirements

A softer overall market tends to mean tighter bids and more competition for nonresidential work. That can bring new names onto your jobs: trade contractors you haven't worked with before, bidding into a segment that's still growing.

New relationships are where insurance gaps hide. Before a new contractor mobilizes:

  1. Check its COI against your project requirements, line by line, not just for a valid policy.
  2. Ask for the additional insured and primary and noncontributory endorsements, not just the certificate.
  3. Track expiration dates from day one, so coverage doesn't lapse mid-project.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against the coverage a project actually requires, for the life of the job.

item.title: Does a project-specific liability policy cover work after the job is built?
item.description: A Texas highway pileup case shows how a liability policy limited to one project's construction work can leave out claims about running the road after it opens.
item.content:encoded:
• Not always. A policy written for one project's construction work may not cover claims about what happens after the project is done, such as operating or maintaining it.
  • In a ruling reported Oct 29, 2026, Liberty Mutual was found to have no duty to defend the builders of a Fort Worth toll road in lawsuits over a 2021 pileup that killed six people.
  • The trial court held that the policy covered bodily injury arising out of work for the project, and that operating and maintaining the road after it opened in 2018 wasn't that work.
  • If a contractor also operates or maintains what it built, check that its coverage reaches that work too, not just the construction phase.

Not always. A liability policy written for one project's construction work can stop short of claims about what happens after the job is built. A Texas highway case reported last week shows how.

The pileup and the policy

On Feb. 11, 2021, a 130-car pileup in a winter storm on I-35W in Fort Worth killed six people and injured about 65, Business Insurance reports. The crash led to dozens of lawsuits against the builders of that stretch of highway, the tollway operator and trucking companies.

The builders, North Tarrant Infrastructure, Ferrovial Construction US and Webber, had a 2013 liability policy from a Liberty Mutual unit for the toll road project. The policy excluded bodily injury arising out of work for any project other than the one it named: rebuilding 6.5 miles of I-35W, building new frontage roads and adding toll lanes. In the district court's words, "the Policy only includes coverage for bodily injury arising out of work conducted for the project."

Why building it wasn't running it

Liberty Mutual defended the builders under a reservation of rights, then sued to get out of the defense. Under Texas's eight-corners rule, the duty to defend turns only on the policy and what the lawsuits allege.

The lawsuits didn't allege the road was built wrong. They alleged failures in operating and maintaining it, including preparing for winter weather. The road opened in 2018, so the district court held that later operation and maintenance couldn't be work "for" a project defined as rebuilding, constructing and expanding the road. Liberty Mutual had no duty to defend.

Business Insurance reports that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit has now affirmed the ruling, and quotes the court calling the policy "clunky and poorly drafted." The district court left one question open: whether Liberty Mutual must pay any judgment. It said that wasn't ripe, since facts at trial could differ from the allegations.

What it means for project requirements

Some projects, like public-private toll roads, have the team that builds them also operate and maintain them. A policy that names a project and its construction work covers that phase. It may not cover the years after.

  1. Read how the policy describes the covered project and the covered work. Narrow descriptions mean narrow coverage.
  2. If a contractor will also operate or maintain the project, ask which policy covers that phase, and get it on file.
  3. Match each phase in your project requirements to a policy that actually reaches it, including completed operations.
  4. Remember a certificate won't show any of this. Get the policy wording or endorsements behind it.

Forsured checks each contractor COI against the coverage a project actually requires, for the life of the job.

item.title: What does "per written contract" mean on an additional insured endorsement?
item.description: Blanket additional insured endorsements add whoever a written contract requires. Whose contract, signed when, and saying what decides whether you're covered.
item.content:encoded:
• "Per written contract" means the policy adds as an additional insured whoever a written contract requires, instead of naming each party on a schedule.
  • Some wording only covers parties the named insured contracted with directly. New York's highest court held in 2018 that "with whom you have agreed" by written contract requires that direct contract.
  • Courts also look at whether the agreement was in writing, whether it was signed before the loss, and whether it really required additional insured status.
  • A certificate doesn't create additional insured status. Get the endorsement, check its wording against your project requirements, and keep the signed contract on file.

"Per written contract" means the policy adds as an additional insured whoever a written contract requires it to add, instead of naming each party on a schedule. It's convenient. One endorsement covers every owner and GC a contractor works for. But it only covers you if your situation fits the endorsement's exact words, and those words differ more than most people expect.

As IA Magazine put it, "There is no such thing as a blanket additional insured endorsement." There are many, and they don't all do the same thing.

Whose contract counts

The biggest question is whether the endorsement covers only parties the named insured contracted with directly.

New York's Court of Appeals answered it for one common wording in 2018. In Gilbane Building Co./TDX Construction Corp. v. St. Paul Fire and Marine Insurance Co., a construction manager on a Manhattan hospital project required each prime contractor to name it as an additional insured. One prime contractor's policy covered any party "with whom you have agreed to add as an additional insured by written contract." The construction manager had no contract of its own with that prime contractor. The court ruled 5-2 that "with" meant the written contract had to be with the additional insured, so the construction manager wasn't covered.

Other wording reaches further. IA Magazine notes that ISO's CG 20 33 requires privity of contract, while CG 20 38 can extend status to parties the contract requires, further up the chain. Courts in other states have split on similar language, IRMI reports, so the same words can mean different things in different places.

When it was signed, and what it says

Wording that requires a written agreement can raise more questions:

  • Is it in writing? Some courts have accepted letters and other written agreements that weren't formal contracts. Others read the requirement strictly.
  • Was it signed in time? Some endorsements require the agreement to be executed before the loss. IRMI notes courts apply that strictly.
  • Does it actually require additional insured status? A contract with a blank or vague insurance section can leave you off the policy.

These fights are still live. In a lawsuit filed in federal court in New York and reported by Insurance Business in July, Berkley alleges Trisura refused to defend a project owner under an endorsement whose schedule read "Per Written Contract." Part of the dispute, as reported, is whether a purchase order's insurance exhibit counts as a written contract. The allegations haven't been decided.

What to check on a contractor COI

  1. Get the endorsement, not just the certificate. As Jones Day noted, additional insured status is created only by an endorsement the insurer issues.
  2. Read the wording. Look for "with whom," "such person or organization," and any execution or timing requirement.
  3. Check it covers every party your project requirements name, including owners and others who don't contract with that contractor directly.
  4. Keep the signed contract, with its insurance requirements, on file next to the endorsement.
  5. Recheck at renewal, when forms can change.

A blanket endorsement is only as good as the contract behind it. Forsured checks each contractor COI and its endorsements against the coverage a project actually requires, for the life of the job.

item.title: Can parametric insurance cover weather delays on a construction project?
item.description: Builder's risk pays for physical damage, not for days lost to cold, heat or wind. A CRC panel explained how parametric cover fills that gap.
item.content:encoded:
• Yes. Parametric policies pay a set amount when a measured trigger is hit, such as a cold, heat, wind, rain or snow threshold, so they can cover weather that halts work without damaging it.
  • Traditional builder's risk covers physical damage only, so lost days, overtime and schedule pressure from weather usually fall on the contractor.
  • Panelists at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference said cover can be tailored to specific operations, such as cold only on concrete pour days or wind only on crane days.
  • Payouts can be used for any purpose, such as funding overtime after a delay.

Yes, it can. Builder's risk insurance pays when weather damages the work. It doesn't pay when weather stops the work. Parametric insurance fills that gap by paying a set amount when a measured trigger is hit at the site, such as a temperature, wind speed or rainfall threshold, whether or not anything was damaged.

That was the case a panel made on Tuesday at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference in National Harbor, as reported by Business Insurance.

The gap builder's risk leaves

Weather stops work long before it breaks anything. Rose Hall, founder of construction risk advisory firm RH Business Ventures, said a day below 40 degrees could cut poured concrete's strength by 50%, and winds above 20 mph can make some crane operations unsafe. Neither shows up as a builder's risk claim.

"Contractors are just absorbing (non-covered weather losses), mostly silently," Hall said.

The panel also pointed to the human cost. Heat-related worker fatalities have risen, and builders often feel pressure to keep working through extreme conditions to stay on schedule.

Cover the days that stop your work

Parametric cover doesn't have to insure every storm. Gary Kaplan, former president of construction at AXA XL, put it this way: "The goal is not to cover every weather event. It is to cover the specific events that stop your specific operations at your specific location."

That means a policy can be shaped around the job:

  • Cold, but only on concrete pour days.
  • Wind, but only on crane days.
  • Payouts that can be used for anything, such as overtime to recover a delay.

Chris Smith, a senior director at the Baldwin Group, said larger builders could use it across a portfolio, and captive owners could use a payout to fund the captive's deductible after a catastrophic event. "To me, this is schedule guardianship," he said.

A better weather number for the bid

Contractors usually set weather allowances in bids from rough estimates. Hall noted that a 10-year average can hide large swings from one year to the next. Kaplan proposed a "zero-weather-day bid," built on site-specific weather estimates, that could give a bidder an edge.

What it means for project requirements

If parametric cover starts showing up in project requirements, it becomes one more line to verify, with its own triggers, limits and named site. As with every coverage, the certificate is only the summary. The policy terms are what pay. Forsured checks each contractor COI against the coverage a project actually requires, for the life of the job.

item.title: What does primary and noncontributory mean on a COI?
item.description: Primary and noncontributory decides whose policy pays first when a contractor's work causes a loss. What it means, which endorsement creates it, and what to check.
item.content:encoded:
• Primary and noncontributory sets the order in which overlapping policies respond: the contractor's policy pays first, and it doesn't ask the additional insured's own policy to share the loss.
  • It's created by an endorsement on the contractor's general liability policy, such as ISO's CG 20 01, not by a line on the certificate.
  • ISO's CG 20 01 applies only when a written contract requires it, and only to the general liability policy. Umbrella and excess need their own wording.
  • On every contractor COI, ask for the endorsement form, check it covers the parties your project requirements name, and check the umbrella too.

Read the insurance section of almost any construction contract and you'll find the same phrase: additional insured coverage "on a primary and noncontributory basis." It's so common it reads like boilerplate. It isn't. It decides whose insurance pays first when a contractor's work causes a loss, and whose loss history takes the hit.

What it means

IRMI describes primary and noncontributory as a term used in contract insurance requirements to set the order in which multiple policies covering the same loss respond. Split it in two:

  • Primary: the contractor's policy responds first to a covered claim against the additional insured, before the additional insured's own policy.
  • Noncontributory: the contractor's policy doesn't ask the additional insured's own insurance to chip in.

Without it, a general liability policy's "other insurance" condition can treat the GC's or owner's own policy as sharing the loss. That's exactly what the contract was written to avoid.

Where it comes from

Like additional insured status, primary and noncontributory is created by policy wording, not by the certificate. A checked box or a note in the description of operations on an ACORD 25 doesn't change the policy.

In 2013 ISO introduced an optional endorsement for it, CG 20 01, "Primary and Noncontributory, Other Insurance Condition." As Claims Journal explained at the time, it was added because so many construction contracts require additional insured coverage on a primary and noncontributory basis. Many carriers use it or their own version, and some blanket additional insured endorsements build similar wording in.

The fine print that trips people up

CG 20 01 comes with two conditions. It applies only when the additional insured is a named insured on another policy, and only when a written contract requires the contractor's coverage to be primary and noncontributory. Missing contract language means missing coverage.

It also amends the general liability policy only. If your project requirements call for primary and noncontributory umbrella or excess coverage, the umbrella needs to say so in its own wording. With umbrella rates still rising, it's an easy gap to miss.

What to check on a contractor COI

  1. Confirm the project requirements actually call for primary and noncontributory, and on which policies (general liability, auto, umbrella).
  2. Ask for the endorsement, not just the certificate. Note the form number and edition.
  3. Check that it covers the parties your requirements name: owner, lender, GC, others.
  4. Check the umbrella or excess policy separately when the requirements extend to it.
  5. Recheck at renewal. Endorsements change when policies renew, and forms keep evolving. "Evolving insurance endorsements" were the backdrop for Cullen and Dykman's session on additional insured endorsements at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference.

It's one line in the contract and one endorsement on the policy. Forsured checks both on every contractor COI, against each project's requirements, for the life of the job.

item.title: What we heard at our first IRMI Construction Risk Conference
item.description: Forsured spent IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference talking COIs with brokers, carriers and contractors. Five things we heard, and what we're doing about them.
item.content:encoded:
• Forsured spent IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference in National Harbor meeting brokers, carriers and contractors about contractor COIs.
  • The loudest complaint: today's COI tools throw too many red alerts and reject certificates over small issues without explaining what actually matters.
  • Brokers and carriers want contractor COI data they can bring to renewals and share with clients, not more paperwork.
  • Neutral wording, "project requirements" and "contractor COIs", landed with general contractors and trade contractors alike, so that's how we talk now.

This week Forsured showed up at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference at the Gaylord National in National Harbor. It was our first CRC. We weren't on the sponsor list and we didn't have a booth. We had a mix of black and white Forsured polos, an independent field guide to the conference, a short video about catching the COI gap, and one question for everyone we met: what happens to a contractor COI after it's filed?

The answers were consistent enough that we want to share them. Nobody below is named, because these were hallway conversations, not interviews.

1. Too many red alerts, not enough answers

The complaint we heard most came from people already paying for COI tracking. Their tools flag everything. Certificates get rejected over small formatting issues, contractors get frustrated, and the alerts that matter (a lapsed policy, an umbrella below the project requirement, an additional insured endorsement without completed operations) get lost in the noise.

What they want is a review that reads the certificate and the endorsements the way a risk manager would, ranks what actually exposes the project, and says why.

2. Brokers want data for renewals

Brokers told us the same thing in different words: show me what my client's contracts actually required last year, and how often their contractors fell short. With umbrella and excess rates still rising (WTW expects another 5% to 15% in 2027), walking into a renewal with that data is worth more than another stack of certificates.

3. Carriers care how contractors manage the trades they hire

Underwriters are paying attention to contractor management. Carrier teams we spoke with were interested in tools they could point their construction insureds to, because a contractor that checks every COI against project requirements is a better risk.

4. Big projects are still run on spreadsheets

Some of the largest projects represented at CRC still track contractor insurance in spreadsheets and inboxes. Certificates arrive in different formats from different countries, and the people responsible know they can't see the whole picture.

5. The words matter

We came in using the general contractor's shorthand for the paperwork. By the end of day 1 we'd switched to "project requirements" and "contractor COIs." The neutral wording works for general contractors, trade contractors and owners alike, and it describes the real job: every contractor, checked against what the project requires.

What's next

We're following up with everyone who asked to see Forsured on their own paperwork. If we didn't get to meet you at the Gaylord, the offer is the same: a free COI risk check, no strings attached. Send one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two to hello@forsured.ai, and we'll walk you through every gap we find.

We'll also keep writing here every weekday about what's moving in construction insurance and contractor COI compliance. Thank you to IRMI and everyone in National Harbor who stopped to talk.

item.title: A COI on file isn't proof of coverage
item.description: A certificate of insurance shows what a contractor bought on one day. Here's what it can't tell you, and what to check against your project requirements instead.
item.content:encoded:
• A certificate of insurance is evidence that a policy existed when it was issued. The standard ACORD 25 form says it confers no rights on the certificate holder.
  • Additional insured status, waivers and primary and noncontributory wording live in the policy endorsements, not on the certificate.
  • Policies lapse, renew with new terms and get re-endorsed mid-project, so a COI that passed review in March can be out of compliance by July.
  • The fix is to check each contractor COI against the project's actual requirements, ask for the endorsements, and keep checking for the life of the job.

Every general contractor has a folder of contractor COIs. Most of them have been looked at once, by someone in a hurry, at the moment the contractor was onboarded. The certificate was there, the boxes were checked, and the work started.

That folder feels like protection. It usually isn't, at least not the way people assume.

What a certificate of insurance actually is

IRMI defines a certificate of insurance as a document providing evidence that certain general types of insurance have been bought, along with the types of coverage and limits. That is the whole job of the document: evidence, on the day it was issued.

The standard ACORD 25 certificate says so on its face. It is "issued as a matter of information only and confers no rights upon the certificate holder," and it does not amend, extend or alter the coverage of the policies listed. If the certificate and the policy disagree, the policy wins.

Where the gap hides

The endorsements. Additional insured status, waivers of subrogation and primary and noncontributory wording are created by endorsements on the contractor's policy. A checked "ADDL INSD" box on a certificate is not the endorsement. And endorsement forms keep changing, a point Cullen and Dykman's Christopher Ruggiero made in his session on decoding additional insured endorsements at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference: the coverage you negotiate in the contract only holds if the endorsement on the policy matches it.

The dates. Policies lapse, get cancelled for nonpayment and renew with new terms. A contractor COI that cleared prequalification in March can be out of compliance by July, and nobody finds out until there's a claim.

The limits. Project requirements often call for higher umbrella limits than a contractor carries on its standard program. With umbrella and excess rates still climbing (WTW expects another 5% to 15% in 2027), that is exactly the line where contractors trim.

The fine print in the requirements themselves. Owners and lenders write requirements that differ project to project. A certificate that satisfies one job can fail the next one across the street.

What to check instead

  1. Start from the project's requirements, not a generic checklist. Each project has its own limits, endorsements and wording.
  2. Compare every contractor COI against those requirements line by line: coverage types, limits, policy dates, and the named insured matching the contracting entity.
  3. Ask for the endorsements that the requirements depend on, and read the form numbers and wording, not just the box on the certificate.
  4. Track expirations and renewals so a policy that changes mid-project gets reviewed again.
  5. When something's missing, bring the contractor's broker into the fix early, while it's a paperwork problem and not a claim.

Why it matters more now

Carriers notice. WTW's 2027 construction outlook says underwriters give favorable consideration to contractors with strong management of the trade partners they hire. A file full of unchecked certificates says the opposite.

That's the work Forsured does: check each contractor COI against your project requirements, flag the gaps, and keep checking for the life of the job.

item.title: 3 takeaways from day 2 of IRMI's Construction Risk Conference
item.description: Additional insured endorsements, prequalification as a snapshot, and insurance data you can't search. What we were digging into on day 2 at IRMI CRC 2026.
item.content:encoded:
• Additional insured coverage only holds if the endorsement on the contractor's policy matches the project requirements, and endorsement forms keep changing.
  • Prequalification checks insurance once. Policies renew, lapse and get re-endorsed mid-project, so compliance has to be checked continuously.
  • Contractor COIs stored as PDFs can't be trended, audited or shared with a broker or carrier at renewal.

Day 2 at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference is a wrap. Three things we were digging into on Tuesday.

1. The endorsement is the contract's last line of defense

Tuesday opened with "Decoding Additional Insured Endorsements for Successful Contractual Risk Transfer," led by Christopher Ruggiero, partner and construction litigation chair at Cullen and Dykman. His preview made a point every GC should hear: as claim costs rise, the indemnity and additional insured coverage you negotiate is harder to secure, because the endorsement forms keep changing.

The coverage you negotiated only holds if the endorsement on the contractor's policy actually matches your project requirements. A checked box on a COI doesn't tell you that. The form number and its wording do.

2. Prequalification is a snapshot. Insurance is a moving target.

"The Prequalification Puzzle" was on Tuesday's agenda, and it's a good reminder of how much happens after a contractor clears prequal. A contractor COI that passed in March can be out of compliance by July. Policies renew with new terms, lapse for nonpayment and get re-endorsed mid-project.

Prequalification answers "can this firm do the work?" It was never built to answer "is this firm covered today, for this project?"

3. Insurance data you can't search is its own risk

Contractor COIs sitting as PDFs in an inbox can't be trended, audited or shared with your broker or carrier when renewal comes around. "When Data Becomes Risk" was on the afternoon agenda, and that's the version of it we see most: the information exists, but nobody can answer a simple question like "which of our active contractors carry less umbrella than the job requires?"

Structured COI data turns that into a two-minute answer, and it's the same data a carrier wants to see when it asks how you manage the trades you hire.

If you want that answer for one of your own projects, start with one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two.

item.title: IRMI is rewriting its design-build risk and insurance guide
item.description: IRMI picked American Global to rewrite its Design-Build Risk and Insurance guide. What the update covers, and what design-build means for contractor COI review.
item.content:encoded:
• IRMI selected brokerage American Global to rewrite its Design-Build Risk and Insurance guide, edited by IRMI's Megan Jolly.
  • The update covers progressive design-build, risk allocation, indemnification, limits of liability, professional liability, project-specific coverage and bonding.
  • On design-build work, check contractor COIs for professional liability wherever a contractor carries design responsibility, not just general liability.

The International Risk Management Institute (IRMI) has picked American Global, a construction and infrastructure risk and insurance brokerage, to rewrite its long-running Design-Build Risk and Insurance guide. The team includes Caryn Maxfield, Ante Petricevic, François Wasselin and Giovanni Bach, with IRMI's Megan Jolly editing, according to the October 23 announcement.

What the update covers

The rewrite is meant to catch up with how design-build is delivered today, including progressive design-build. It covers contractual risk allocation, indemnification, limits of liability, professional liability insurance, project-specific coverage and bonding.

Why it matters for contractor COIs

Design-build shifts design responsibility to the builder's side of the contract. That has a direct effect on what a compliant contractor COI looks like:

  • Professional liability enters the picture. A design-builder, and any trade contractor doing delegated design on mechanical, electrical, structural steel or curtain wall scopes, may need professional liability that a general liability policy won't provide.
  • Requirements differ by role. The same project can need different coverage from a designer, a design-builder and a build-only trade contractor. One template for every firm misses that.
  • Project-specific programs change the checklist. When an owner or contractor buys project-specific coverage, contractor COIs have to be checked against what the program does and doesn't cover.

WTW's 2027 outlook expects contractor's professional liability to run flat to up 5% on annual programs and flat to up 10% on project-specific policies, so the coverage is available. The job is making sure the contractors who need it actually carry it, at the limits the project requires.

IRMI's guides are a standard reference for construction risk teams, and this one is worth reading when it lands.

item.title: How to check a contractor COI against your project requirements
item.description: A practical checklist for checking a contractor certificate of insurance against one project's requirements: coverages, limits, dates and endorsements.
item.content:encoded:
• Start from the project's insurance requirements, not a generic template. Limits and endorsements differ by owner, lender and contract.
  • Check five things on every COI: named insured, coverage types and limits, policy dates, endorsements, and the certificate holder.
  • Ask for the actual endorsement forms when the contract requires additional insured status, waiver of subrogation or primary and noncontributory wording.
  • Recheck at every renewal and before every expiration. A one-time review misses most of the gaps that matter.

Most COI reviews fail for one reason: the certificate gets checked against a generic template instead of the requirements of the project the contractor is actually working on. Here is the checklist we use, in order.

Before you open the certificate

Pull the insurance section of the contract or the project's insurance requirements exhibit. Write down, for this project:

  • Each required coverage (general liability, auto, workers' compensation and employer's liability, umbrella or excess, and anything trade-specific like professional or pollution liability)
  • The minimum limit for each, including whether umbrella must follow form
  • Required endorsements: additional insured (ongoing and completed operations), waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory
  • Who must be named as additional insured: owner, lender, GC, others
  • How long completed operations coverage must be maintained after the job

The five checks

1. Named insured

The named insured on the certificate should match the legal entity on the contract. A parent company, a DBA or a sister company is a gap until someone confirms the right entity is covered.

2. Coverages and limits

Compare every line against the requirements. Umbrella and excess is where shortfalls show up most, because project requirements often call for more than a trade contractor carries on its standard program.

3. Policy dates

Every policy should be in force for the work. Note each expiration date, and plan to recheck before it, not after.

4. Endorsements

A box on the certificate is not an endorsement. When the contract requires additional insured status, a waiver of subrogation or primary and noncontributory wording, ask for the endorsement forms and read them. Check that additional insured coverage includes completed operations when the contract requires it. Endorsement forms change often, so the form number matters.

5. Certificate holder and description

The certificate holder should be correct, and the description of operations should reference the project or the contract where your requirements ask for it.

When you find a gap

Send the contractor's broker the specific requirement that isn't met, quoted from the project requirements, and the line on the certificate or endorsement that falls short. Specific asks get fixed in days. Vague ones ("please send an updated COI") come back with the same certificate.

Keep it current

A COI review is only as good as its date. Recheck when a policy renews, when a certificate is reissued, and ahead of every expiration. On a long project that means continuous monitoring, which is what Forsured does for every contractor on every active project.

item.title: 3 takeaways from day 1 of IRMI's Construction Risk Conference
item.description: Crowded bids and thin margins, umbrella rates still rising, and contractor management turning into an underwriting factor. What stuck with us from day 1 at IRMI CRC 2026.
item.content:encoded:
• Bids are crowded: ABC chief economist Anirban Basu says jobs that once drew 2 to 4 bids now draw as many as 12 to 16, and about a third of contractors expect margins to shrink.
  • WTW expects umbrella and excess rates to rise another 5% to 15% in 2027, and brokers want renewal data on how often contracts demand high umbrella limits.
  • Carriers give favorable consideration to strong management of the contractors a firm hires, so contractor COI compliance is becoming an underwriting story.

Day 1 at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference in National Harbor is in the books. Here are the three things that stuck with us from Monday, and what each one means for anyone collecting contractor COIs.

1. Margins are thin, and bids are crowded

Anirban Basu, chief economist at Associated Builders and Contractors, opened CRC's Monday general session. His recent numbers, reported by Construction Dive, set the tone: projects that once drew two to four bids are now drawing as many as 12 to 16, and about 32% of contractors surveyed expect profit margins to decline over the next year, up from 26% in July.

When the low bid wins, a contractor's insurance gap isn't a paperwork problem. It's a margin problem. A trade contractor that trimmed its umbrella to sharpen a number is the one whose gap lands back on the GC's program after a loss.

2. Umbrella is where the pain is

WTW expects umbrella and excess rates for construction to rise another 5% to 15% in 2027, the same range it gives auto liability, while general liability runs flat to up 10%.

A broker we sat down with asked for something simple: show me how many of last year's contracts required a high umbrella limit, so I can walk into renewal with data instead of guesses. That data exists in every GC's contractor COI file. It just isn't searchable when the certificates are PDFs in an inbox.

3. Contractor management is becoming an underwriting factor

WTW's outlook says carriers give favorable underwriting consideration to firms with strong management of the trades they hire, alongside loss experience and fleet controls. "When Compliance Isn't Coverage" was on Monday's agenda for a reason: a contractor COI in a file isn't proof of coverage, and underwriters know it.

For a GC, that turns COI review from back-office cleanup into something you can show a carrier at renewal: every contractor checked against project requirements, every gap tracked to a fix.

Want to see what your own contractor COI file would tell a carrier? That's what our free COI risk check is for.

item.title: What the 2027 construction insurance outlook means for contractor COIs
item.description: WTW forecasts construction umbrella and excess rates up 5% to 15% in 2027. Here's the full outlook by line, and why it raises the stakes on contractor COI review.
item.content:encoded:
• WTW's 2027 outlook for construction: umbrella and excess up 5% to 15%, auto up 5% to 15%, general liability flat to up 10%, workers' compensation flat to up 5%.
  • Lead umbrella and excess on wrap-up programs (OCIPs and CCIPs) is also expected up 5% to 15%.
  • When umbrella costs rise, trade contractors are tempted to carry less than project requirements demand, so umbrella is the line to check first on every contractor COI.
  • Carriers favor firms with strong management of the contractors they hire, which makes a clean contractor COI record useful at renewal.

WTW published its Insurance Marketplace Realities 2027 report for construction on October 1. The headline for anyone managing contractor COIs: most lines are steady, and the expensive one keeps getting more expensive.

The outlook by line

CoverageWTW 2027 forecast
Umbrella and excess liabilityUp 5% to 15%
Auto liabilityUp 5% to 15%
General liabilityFlat to up 10%
Workers' compensationFlat to up 5%
Project-specific builders risk (non-high hazard)Down 2.5% to up 2.5%
Master builders riskDown 5% to up 5%
Contractor's professional liability (annual)Flat to up 5%
Wrap-ups (OCIP and CCIP), lead umbrella and excessUp 5% to 15%

Umbrella has been the pressure point for years

This isn't new. Back in 2021, ENR reported that umbrella and excess renewals were costing contractors 50% to 100% more, as carriers raised prices, cut limits and raised attachment points. Rates have cooled since then, but umbrella keeps rising faster than the rest of the program.

Why that shows up in your contractor COIs

Project requirements rarely bend to the market. If the contract calls for a $10 million umbrella, it calls for $10 million whether the trade contractor's renewal went up 5% or 15%.

Put that next to a bidding market where, as Construction Dive reported from ABC's Anirban Basu, jobs that once drew 2 to 4 bids are drawing 12 to 16. Thin margins and rising umbrella costs push in the same direction: carry less, and hope nobody checks.

So check umbrella first. On every contractor COI, confirm the umbrella or excess limit meets the project requirement, that it follows form over the underlying policies the contract requires, and that it won't expire before the work is done.

The upside at your own renewal

WTW notes that carriers give favorable underwriting consideration to strong management of the trades a firm hires. A record showing every contractor checked against project requirements, with each gap tracked to a fix, is the kind of evidence an underwriter can use. A folder of unread certificates isn't.
